chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that he
said regarding the attribute of the Eternal: 'He is One, Self-Sufficient, singular in meaning — not with many different meanings.'

He (Muhammad ibn Muslim) said: I said, 'May I be your ransom! A group from the people of Iraq allege that He hears with something other than that with which He sees, and He sees with something other than that with which He hears.'

So he (the Imam) said: 'They have lied and deviated and anthropomorphized. Exalted is God above that! He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing. He hears with that with which He sees, and He sees with that with which He hears.'

He (the narrator) said: I said, 'They allege that He is All-Seeing according to what they themselves comprehend.' So he (the Imam) said: 'Exalted is God! Rather, one comprehends (only) that which has the quality of a creature. And God is not like that.'

key_terms.أَحَدِيُّ الْمَعْنَى: Singular/Unique in meaning — theological term asserting God's attributes are not multiple distinct entities
key_terms.أَلْحَدُوا: They deviated (into heresy/ilhad) — used for those who distort divine attributes
key_terms.الْقَدِيمُ: The Eternal/Pre-existent — divine epithet stressing that God has no beginning
key_terms.سَمِيعٌ بَصِيرٌ: All-Hearing, All-Seeing — divine names from Quran, here interpreted as non-compositional
key_terms.شَبَّهُوا: They anthropomorphized (tashbih) — comparing God to creatures
key_terms.صَمَدٌ: Al-Samad — the Absolute, Self-Sufficient, upon Whom all depend (cf. Quran 112:2)

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Baqir explain the oneness of God's hearing and seeing attributes?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) addresses a crucial theological dispute about divine attributes, specifically hearing and seeing. Against a group from Iraq who argued these are separate distinct faculties in God (implying multiplicity in the Divine Essence), the Imam firmly rejects this as falsehood, heresy, and anthropomorphism. He teaches that God's hearing and seeing are unified — He hears with the very same faculty by which He sees — affirming God's absolute oneness (tawhid) in His essence and attributes, not merely in number.
